title: Ancient 385‑Million‑Year‑Old Amber Discovered in Northwestern China Under UV Light Reveal
body:
A team of Chinese researchers has uncovered the world’s oldest known amber, a 385‑million‑year‑old specimen that dates back to the Late Devonian period, by exposing coal samples from north‑western China to ultraviolet light. The tiny blue‑glowing specks that appeared under the UV lamp turned out to be fossilised resin, pushing the known timeline for amber formation back by more than 100 million years and opening a new window onto the ecosystems that existed before the age of the dinosaurs.

The discovery emerged from an unexpected line of inquiry. While studying the mineral composition of coal seams in the Ordos Basin, scientists noticed that certain dark inclusions emitted a faint blue fluorescence when illuminated with UV radiation. Initial hypotheses ranged from mineral phosphorescence to microbial activity, but detailed spectroscopic analysis revealed the presence of organic compounds characteristic of amber, such as succinic acid and terpenoid markers. Radiometric dating of the surrounding matrix placed the resin at roughly 385 million years old, making it older than the previously oldest amber from the Early Carboniferous of the United Kingdom and the United States.

Amber is more than a decorative gemstone; it is a time capsule that can preserve delicate biological material—trapped insects, plant fragments, and even microscopic microorganisms—intact for hundreds of millions of years. The Devonian period, often called the “Age of Fishes,” also witnessed the first significant colonisation of land by vascular plants and arthropods. Finding amber from this era suggests that resin‑producing plants were already part of these early terrestrial ecosystems, shedding light on the evolution of plant defense mechanisms and the complex interactions between early land flora and fauna.

The implications for paleobiology are profound. If Devonian amber can retain inclusions, scientists may soon be able to examine some of the earliest terrestrial insects and other arthropods in unprecedented detail. Such specimens could answer lingering questions about the timing of insect diversification, the development of flight, and the co‑evolution of plants and pollinators. Moreover, the chemical composition of the resin itself can reveal information about the atmospheric composition of the Devonian, including oxygen levels and the prevalence of certain volatile organic compounds, which in turn influence models of climate and fire regimes in deep time.

The find also underscores the value of interdisciplinary approaches in fossil research. By combining traditional coal geology, advanced spectroscopic techniques, and precise radiometric dating, the team demonstrated that even well‑studied sedimentary formations can still yield surprises. Their methodology may inspire similar UV‑screening surveys of coal and shale deposits worldwide, potentially uncovering more ancient amber deposits that have been overlooked because they lack the classic yellow‑brown hue associated with younger specimens.

Looking ahead, the researchers plan to extract and examine any entrapped organisms within the amber using high‑resolution X‑ray computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy. If successful, these analyses could rewrite parts of the Devonian fossil record, providing the earliest direct evidence of terrestrial arthropod life and their interactions with the nascent forest ecosystems. As the scientific community prepares to peer into this newly opened chapter of Earth’s history, the tiny blue specks that first caught the researchers’ eyes may soon illuminate the origins of life on land in ways previously thought impossible.
